Forcing parties via presidential-called snap-election to take one of two political positions goes against the very idea of free elections, and it is very likely to be struck down by courts. Not only that, but it is also quite unclear that anyone would abide by the results, no matter what they are, since there's also no framework for that.

All the major left-wing figures, as well as the Catalan core of the party have already either retired or left the party during the last couple of years. Local elections were already hard to deal with due to a severe lack of local and regional leadership and grassroots support, and without clear figures to rally around, one can only guess what's next for the PSC.

After an almost decade-long investigatio: After an almost decade-long investigation, the courts have finally reached a verdict regarding the Gürtel case. The case, of incredible complexity, is also tightly linked to the Bárcenas affair, and would explain part of the "B-side financing" of the PP. The head of the operation, Francisco Correa (hence the case name, the literal translation of "Correa", belt, to German), has now been proven to have been running a massive network to funnel illegal kickbacks to the PP across many regions it governed, with the top dogs being Madrid and Valencia. Wealthy businessmen and big contracting companies would, by funding these kickbacks, benefit from rigged public tenders, with instances of these practices going back, at least, to the party's foundation in 1989.

Catalonia finds itself at a political an: Catalonia finds itself at a political and economic crossroads. Catalonia has no special fiscal status a: Catalonia has no special fiscal status as a Spanish Autonomous Community. This means that, unlike the Basque Country or Navarre, Catalonia does not collect its own taxes. Instead, all taxes are collected by the Spanish government and then redistributed to the Autonomous Communities through a complex funding formula. This has always resulted in an acute deficit for Catalonia, with estimates at around €20 billion, close to 8-10% of Catalonia's GDP, or almost half of the Generalitat's annual budget.

Despite the numbers not adding up at all: Despite the numbers not adding up at all, it seems like both {psoe_leader} and {csspa_leader} are still going to submit their proposal to an investiture vote in the Congreso.
Despite the Parlament being legally limi: Despite the Parlament being legally limited in its powers, it is still symbolically the highest representative body of the Catalan people. Using that, we can still push for further action within its walls by passing laws allowing the Generalitat and other official bodies more options. It's no secret that, no matter how water-tight we make these, the Constitutional Court will most probably strike them down.
Despite the PSOE's earlier promises, the: Despite the PSOE's earlier promises, the Congreso ended up modifying more than half of the articles before the approval of the new Statute. Yet still, the biggest blow came from the conservative PP, who challenged the charter in the Constitutional Court. In 2010, the court struck down or reinterpreted 14 articles, including the recognition of Catalonia as a nation, linguistic rights and protections, and wider legislative and fiscal powers. This left many Catalans feel betrayed, which fueled a never-before-seen rise in support for self-determination and independence. Re-gaining strength in 2010 under the motto "We are a nation. We decide.", each September 11th, the National Day of Catalonia, the strength of the independence movement is made visible in the streets, and it only seems to grow stronger.
Despite the Statute of Autonomy already: Despite the Statute of Autonomy already having some minor provisions on the possibility of holding open consultations, this has never been formalized into proper law. The proposed {emphasis1} aims to address this, allowing the President to call for any sort of non-binding consultation. It is bound to be a controversial law nonetheless. {clause1}{clause2}
Despite us being the original proponents: Despite us being the original proponents, ERC and CiU have made many amendments to the text to make it more palatable to moderate parties by adding explicit mentions of Legality, Dialogue, and Europeism.

Francisco Franco's victory in the Spanis: Francisco Franco's victory in the Spanish Civil War brought about a brutal fascist national-catholic dictatorship that lasted until his death in 1975. Its repression hits particularly hard on political dissent, and specially that coming from the "peripheral nationalities" of Spain, including Catalonia. The dictatorship imposes cultural and linguistic repression, banning Catalan language teaching, writing and speaking; and executing or exiling leaders like the republican President Lluís Companys.

From the depths of the Spanish political: From the depths of the Spanish political spectrum, Vox seems to be climbing up the polls ever so steadily, and now we're reaching a point where they may very well get an important share of the seats in the Congreso. With a heavy dose of nostalgia for the Franco-era Spain and tubro-charged chauvinistic nationalism, Vox is openly demanding the abolition of the autonomy-based State in favour of re-centralization, the mass deportation of immigrants, a ban on any party or organization seeking independence from Spain, and cuts to women and LGBTQ+ rights, among many others.
From the street protests of Barcelona, t: From the street protests of Barcelona, to the town hall with BComu and Ada Colau, now Jaume Asens will take the reigns of a renewed CECP. At least he seems to conserve a bit o the federalist spirit that CSQP embodied...
From the street-filling anti-austerity p: From the street-filling anti-austerity protests around Spain, a new space in the left seems to have appeared to challenge the dominance of the PSOE. Led by Pablo Iglesias, Podemos so far has broken away from many of the conventions of the traditional Spanish left, advocating for a system-wide re-structuring.

However, it seems unlikely that the Spanish Gobierno presided by Mariano Rajoy will agree to such deal, and much less in times of hardship also for the wider Spanish and European economies.

The supposed white envelopes would have included monthly under-the-table payments of up to €15.000 per person.

Route to Ítaca is about imagining how di: Route to Ítaca is about imagining how different could the 2010's have been for Catalonia, had things worked even so slightly differently. Its point is not to create a pro-independence fantasy, but rather, to serve as a tool to reflect on how far certain political movements got during the 2010's, and how further could they have gone. It's about the independence movement, but also about the anti-austerity struggles that plagued Europe, and many other street-born potentially revolutionary forces for change in the 21st century that ultimately folded into the status quo. What can hindsight provide, and what issues remain even then? Those are the enormous questions that (spoiler) will remain open even as you complete all the paths.
